doc.title: Charles McPherson interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 9, 2024 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Hearing Charlie Parker and Jimmy Heath's compliment
summary: He recalls the Parker 'linear logic' that made sense at 14-15, and reacts to Jimmy Heath's quote about his Parker language.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Yeah you take me back to you had told a story about hearing Charlie Parker play “Tico Tico” and that it made sense to you.
That was so interesting that it just made sense to you. And you said, “I knew immediately that this is what I wanted to do.”

Yes. Right. That’s true. Yeah. And I think a lot of people felt that when they first heard Charlie Parker. I’m not the only one. But when I first heard Bird, yeah, that was overwhelming because it made perfect sense to me. And there was something about the way — because he played a lot of notes, but a lot of people played a lot of notes but I could hear the linear logic with Charlie Parker. I could tell — and I couldn’t — I would never use terms like that — “linear logic” or — I wouldn’t use that term. I wouldn’t even know what that was when I’m 15, 14 years old. But I could understand it, let’s put it that

way. It made sense to me. And so that was what got me. It was compelling. And I got it. I couldn’t say what it was, I couldn’t use the right verbiage or the right semantics to describe — I knew nothing about harmony or theory or any of that. I did know major scales. I could play the major scales but I didn’t know anything about the cycle of fifths or any of that you know. But I could tell that he connected these long sentences and they were like perfectly, seamlessly connected. And then the logic of it was apparent to me, and that’s what got me.

I have a quote here I want to read from the late Jimmy Heath. It says, “I think Charles McPherson is the number one saxophonist who has incorporated the Charlie Parker language. He has this quality of eruption in his lines, he has that Charlie Parker language and he’s still himself. He’s so far inside of the part nobody else gets, that you would have to say it’s amazing.”
Oh well I didn’t know he said that, that is really a nice compliment.
Yeah that is a very nice — in fact yeah, that’s a nice one.
I think I’ll send that to you.

Yeah, that is beautiful. I mean it’s self-serving that I say that, but coming from a great musician like him, and a wonderful, wonderful saxophonist and wonderful composer, that was around during the really golden age. You know his age really was privy to all of the great musicians before Charlie Parker. These people were still around and still living, and he’s heard these people in person. It’s not abstract for his — what was he born, 19 what 29 or 28? I don’t know somewhere probably 1926, 27, whatever it is. But that age of those people, that generation, were privy to all these great saxophone players, trumpets, big bands, you know just all — everybody was still living pretty much. So he’s a great musician and his playing and his writing reflects his natural talent but it also reflects all of this great music that he absorbed. So that’s — a compliment from him is very special.
